controls.statement: Assign a business owner and technical steward to every material data domain and data product.

Review data risk when introducing new sources, joins, inferences, models, or destinations.
Make data incidents, quality failures, and rights requests routable to accountable owners.
Measure governance by risk and data outcomes rather than catalog completion alone.
Resolve conflicting definitions through an authoritative governance process.
Ensure suppliers and processors meet equivalent data obligations.
Remove orphaned stores, copies, exports, accounts, and pipelines.
Preserve evidence of data decisions and changes.
Review governance as products, jurisdictions, users, and purposes evolve.
Model domain concepts and relationships independently of a specific storage technology before physical optimization.
Use a shared vocabulary and define every material entity, attribute, identifier, status, unit, and relationship.
Distinguish natural, surrogate, external, display, tenant, and correlation identifiers.
Define null, absent, unknown, not-applicable, zero, empty, and deleted semantics explicitly.
Encode invariants through schema and constraints where enforcement is reliable.
Normalize authoritative data enough to avoid contradictory facts, and denormalize only with ownership and reconciliation.
Define cardinality, optionality, uniqueness, referential, temporal, and lifecycle constraints.
Choose precision, scale, encoding, collation, normalization, time zone, and unit deliberately.
Represent history and effective time where past truth or auditability matters.
Separate immutable facts from mutable projections and current-state summaries.
Align partitions, tenancy, residency, and encryption boundaries with governance requirements.
Model access patterns without making one query pattern corrupt the domain model.
Avoid polymorphic or untyped structures that hide incompatible meanings without governance.
Version schemas and define compatibility for producers and consumers.
Document ownership and source of truth for every duplicated field.
Design deletion and legal hold into relationships rather than relying on ad hoc cleanup.
Make bulk import, export, correction, and migration semantics explicit.
Validate models with representative data volumes, edge cases, and users.
Prevent internal storage layout from becoming an unnecessary public contract.
Review the model when workarounds and repeated joins show a mismatch with the domain.
Define quality dimensions and thresholds according to each intended use and consequence of error.
Identify critical data elements and the business rules they must satisfy.
Validate at collection and ingestion while preserving raw evidence needed for investigation.
Distinguish invalid, missing, late, duplicated, contradictory, stale, inferred, and uncertain data.
Record provenance, collection time, effective time, processing time, and quality status where material.
Use referential, domain, uniqueness, range, format, temporal, and cross-field checks.
Reconcile counts, totals, balances, checksums, and invariants across boundaries.
Monitor drift, schema change, source change, late arrival, and silent truncation.
Segment quality by source, cohort, region, tenant, device, and time when aggregate metrics hide problems.
Prevent downstream systems from treating unknown or low-confidence values as authoritative.
Provide quarantine, correction, replay, and backfill procedures.
Preserve audit history for material corrections.
Assign owners and response objectives to failed quality rules.
Test pipelines with malformed, boundary, duplicate, reordered, late, and partial data.
Measure false positives and false negatives in automated quality checks.
Communicate freshness, completeness, and limitations to consumers.
Prevent remediation from destroying evidence or creating inconsistent copies.
Verify that derived metrics remain semantically valid after source or transformation changes.
Use user and operator reports as quality signals.
Retire quality rules that no longer correspond to a real information need, and add rules from incidents and escaped defects.
Catalog material data sets, streams, schemas, metrics, reports, models, features, and exports.
Record owner, steward, purpose, source, consumers, sensitivity, residency, retention, quality, and support status.
Maintain business definitions and technical schemas together with clear authority.
Capture lineage across ingestion, transformation, aggregation, model use, export, and deletion.
Version metadata and retain historical meaning for past reports and incidents.
Make lineage granular enough to assess impact without exposing unnecessary sensitive values.
Connect code, configuration, jobs, schemas, tests, dashboards, and incidents to data assets.
Detect undocumented stores, fields, pipelines, and transfers.
Mark deprecated, experimental, untrusted, sampled, synthetic, and derived assets clearly.
Expose freshness, quality, completeness, and known limitations to consumers.
Control access to sensitive metadata that could reveal identities, vulnerabilities, or business secrets.
Use automated discovery as assistance, not a substitute for accountable validation.
Review lineage after schema, source, transformation, supplier, or model changes.
Ensure deletion, consent, and legal-hold propagation can be traced.
Support impact analysis before breaking or retiring an asset.
Prevent multiple conflicting definitions of critical business measures.
Make catalog search and terminology understandable to non-specialist users.
Define metadata retention and retirement.
Measure catalog accuracy, coverage, use, stale ownership, and unresolved quality issues.
Verify metadata against deployed reality periodically.
Classify each change as additive, compatible, breaking, destructive, reparative, or behavioral.
